answer.reason: Mainly speech: Ulla's slight, Rav Hamnuna's shame and Ulla's rehabilitating reply. The shame is an emotional event, there is conflict and a resolution, but almost everything happens in dialogue.
A case brought to Rabbi, who gave no ruling. Coming before him is the only event, and segment 3 is the Gemara's explanation.
The brother's attempt to disqualify the yevama is a dispute carried on almost entirely in dialogue (offers and fears), with conflict but no narrated outcome.
A report of Rav Huna's habitual practice when litigants came, cited as precedent, with no one-time event and nothing following.
Rav and Rav Yehuda walking behind a woman: a setting, then a dialogue with some tension. Mainly speech with little narrated action or change.
Rabba bar Avuh's instruction is quoted inside the legal give-and-take to test an opinion. Nothing is narrated as having happened.

Incident plus ruling: the brewer betroths with someone else's sediment, the owner finds him and comments, and Rava rules. There is more than coming before a rabbi, but little change beyond the ruling.
Aher sees Hutzpit's tongue dragged in the street, reacts and goes out to sin. Event, reaction and a causal change, about a post-biblical sage.
Reports of sages who visited and ruled on cases. Each is an incident followed only by a ruling, transmitted as halakhic testimony.
An eyewitness measurement of a place, cited as part of a legal objection. No incident is narrated.
R. Yohanan expounds, R. Elazar refutes him and he falls silent, then Reish Lakish exposes the source and R. Yohanan goes and masters Torat Kohanim. Several actions, conflict and a change.
A yevama came before R. Tarfon and he gave an instruction. The arrival is the only event, followed by a ruling, cited as a source for the law.
A bare report of how Rabba bar Hiyya conducted halitza, with Shmuel's critical remark. That is ordinary scholarly criticism, with no continuation or change.
A visit that only frames a halakhic question and answer about carrying. The setting is not a second event (Shabbat 147a line).
Rav Anan answers a question by pointing to Shmuel's habitual silence about the Neharde'a gates. This is practice cited as evidence, not an event.
A baraita's argument cites the fact that many were recircumcised in Bar Kokhba's days as evidence. It is a general historical report inside legal debate, not a narrated incident.
A report of a household practice in R. Pedat's house and his ruling that the beam is a utensil. It is a habitual practice that leads nowhere.
A one-line mention of a precedent case and the ruling requiring halitza. The incident is barely told and nothing else happens.

The Gemara cites an incident in which a suspected man passed his in-laws' door and Rav Sheshet flogged him. These are two real acts, but the incident is only alluded to as an objection within legal discussion.
Two brief precedents (Rav Kahana valuing a cloth, Mar bar Rav Ashi buying one at a premium) are cited as legal evidence. Each is a single act with no development.
The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's halitza incident (how it was known, where it happened); this is legal commentary on a story told elsewhere, not a story.
Rav Malkiyyu marries off the deaf-mute and writes a ketubah, then Rava praises his reasoning; real events but little change or consequence.
A baraita alludes to a single incident followed only by the Sages' ruling validating it; one event and a ruling with nothing else narrated.
Ravnai reports a halakha, Ameimar praises it and Rav Ashi rebukes him; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, which Jeff ruled is not a story (Ketubot 21b:0).
A deposit and the bailee's death without instruction, then the case before Rav Nahman and his ruling; an incident with a ruling but little further action or change.
Bonyos sends a measure and Rabbi measures it; two events but weak causality and little change, cited as a metrological datum.
Mainly an exchange of words between the Rabbis and R. Abba bar Zavda, with the event of his becoming impotent mentioned as explanation inside the legal give-and-take.
A setting (R. Yehoshua visits R. Yohanan ben Nuri among the trees) followed by a question and answer; per the Shabbat 147a ruling a setting plus Q&A is not a story.
Jeff ruled this passage (Ketubot 65a:10) borderline: the courtroom apportioning of wine is a little more than a ruling.
A deposit followed by a dispute in dialogue between depositor and bailee; one event, then conflict in speech, with the resolution outside the passage.

A historical account of the priestly court changing and restoring the ketubah ordinance in response to behavior; events and change, but told as legal history by collective actors with no narrated scene.
The superintendent refuses to rent, the neighbors go to three rabbis in turn until Rav Yehuda rules; some action beyond the ruling, but mainly a case brought for a halakhic answer.
Rav Yosef forgot a teaching and Abaye reminds him; the passage is a scholarly exchange over the content of the halakha with no event beyond speech.
A described yard prompts Abaye and Rava to discuss possible halakhic solutions; legal discussion with no narrated event.
A man rents out a millstone, becomes rich, buys his own millstone and donkey, and demands money, leading to a dispute; several actions, change and conflict, an incident that leads to a ruling.
A deposit and Rav Dimi's death without instruction, then the case before Rabbi Abba and his ruling; incident plus ruling with little further change.
Shmuel crosses on a ferry, a man helps him, reveals he has a case, and Shmuel disqualifies himself; actions, causality and a change in outcome.
Mainly a halakhic challenge, but Rava goes out and shows Rav Safra the submerged wall foundations, an action that resolves it.
A woman seizes a cup and comes before Rava, who rules; one event then a ruling whose outcome is only implied, which Jeff ruled is not a story (2026-10-25).
Rav Nahman comes and instructs that the earth be cleared, followed by legal analysis of his view; a single instruction with nothing following.
A setting (missed the study hall, met R. Asi) framing a question and answer about a ruling; like Shabbat 147a, not enough for a story.
The superintendent refuses to rent, the neighbours come before R. Zeira and he cites a ruling; one event then a ruling, with nothing changing afterwards.
A man whose betrothed died comes before the rabbis, who rule, and the passage turns to legal discussion; one event followed by a ruling.
R. Elazar b. Tzadok's family practice on one Ninth of Av is cited as evidence for a halakhic point; a report of what was done, with no response or development.
Rav's ruling at Damharya is only alluded to as precedent within a scholarly dispute; a report of a ruling cited as evidence, inside ordinary debate.
The Mishnah's incident is only referenced ('etc.'); the passage is the Gemara's discussion of why it counts as miraculous, commentary on a story told elsewhere.
A man betroths with a myrtle branch, the question is sent to Rav Yosef, who rules; one event then a ruling, with no outcome narrated.
They came before R. Ami and he ruled; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
The rabbis press Rav Sheshet to marry and he deflects, with the Gemara supplying that he had become impotent from Rav Huna's long discourses; mainly speech with some tension and an event mentioned.
A man deposits pearls with R. Meyasha, who dies without instructions, and the parties come before R. Ami who awards them; narrated events plus a resolving ruling, like the cow case.
Ben Azzai's finding a genealogy scroll is a single act reported to introduce its contents; nothing follows from it.
Rabba bar bar Hana gives Rav money to buy land and Rav buys it for himself; two actions with conflict and change, though the Gemara's justifications are commentary.
Abaye's boast and a sage's challenge followed by a baraita; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth with no event.
A widow's son asks R. Eliezer, then goes to R. Yehoshua, who answers him sarcastically; mainly speech with some movement and a barbed exchange.
R. Shabbtai's daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag of coins and the Sages could not take it from her; a real incident, but only briefly reported as evidence for the ruling.
Two deeds come before Rav Yosef, he rules and the losing party argues; a case before a rabbi with ruling and discussion, no other narrated event or change.
Rav Huna tears silk before his son to test whether he will get angry; a real act with intent, but the outcome is not narrated and the Gemara turns to commentary.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna b. R. Yehoshua conducted halitza before five; a bare report of a practice cited to explain the law.
The judges report that Rav Yehuda ruled in a case of branches; an incident only alluded to as a precedent, with no narrated development.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa for oxen, no longer needs the money, and Rav Pappa returns the land; several actions and a change.
The sages gather in Lod, a question is put, they disagree and then reach a joint conclusion. It is almost all speech, with some conflict and a resolution, so borderline.
Relatives come before R. Yohanan, who advises them, and he later regrets helping them. That is mostly a ruling, but his change of mind adds some change, so borderline rather than not.
Statements by Rav and R. Hiyya about their own eiruv practice. Speech cited as a legal source, with no event.
A setting (Ravina finds Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door) that only frames a legal dilemma. Under the Shabbat 147a ruling a setting plus a question is not a story.
A case comes before the Sages and they rule. Coming before them is the only event, which is R-C0's limit.
Cases came before Rabbi and R. Yishmael and they ruled, followed by scholarly discussion of the rulings. There is no event beyond bringing the case and no real conflict.

A man's incidental remark about his and his mother's captivity leads Rabbi to permit her to marry into the priesthood. It is essentially a case and a ruling, but the narrated captivity and the change in her status keep it borderline.
An incident alluded to inside the legal discussion: a man held a feast on the ninetieth day and Rava made him forfeit it. The ruling is an act with a consequence, but the incident is only sketched.
A man testifies before R. Ami, they exchange questions and answers, and R. Ami rules. Coming before the rabbi and his ruling is all that happens.
Rav Yosef says he has not heard a teaching and Abaye reminds him that he taught it. Ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.
One line of background (Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya) with no event in the passage itself.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with an orphan's beer, given as his practice and reasoning. Nothing follows from it.
An incident cited as evidence: the tumtum of Biri was operated on and later fathered seven children. It has events and change but is only alluded to inside a legal argument.
Minyamin's statement of his own status and his marriage plans, cited as a legal source. It is speech and intention, not a narrated event.
The students ask R. Eliezer a question and he answers. The register rules this exact passage (Yevamot 78b:9) not a story.

An incident only alluded to: a debtor hid his money behind a gentile, so the Sages forced him to sell his land. It has an action and a consequence but is recounted only briefly inside legal discussion.
Two linked incidents before Reish Lakish and R. Yohanan. Reish Lakish realizes R. Elazar had withheld the source, looks at him harshly and rebukes him: conflict, an emotional reaction and a change.
Rav Yosef says he has not heard a teaching and Abaye recites what he had taught them. Scholarly dialogue with no narrated event.
One act (residents put a rolled mat in an alleyway in Sura) followed only by Rav Hisda's legal critique. Nothing else happens.

A dialogue between R. Yohanan and R. Elazar with disagreement, R. Yohanan's grief, and R. Elazar finding him a remedy. It is mainly speech but has conflict and an emotional change, like Ketubot 112a:11.
A man snatches a belt from a seller, proposes betrothal, she takes it back in silence, and Rav Nahman rules. Several narrated actions followed by a ruling, like the cow case.
The Sages apportion wine to Nakdimon's daughter-in-law, she blesses them and they withhold amen. The ruling is itself an act that changes something, but it is a thin courtroom incident (Ketubot 65a).
During a famine the Sages ask Rav Yosef to pray and he declines. One real event as the setting, then mainly speech with some tension.
A man betrothed a minor with vegetables in the market, then Ravina rules. One act followed by a ruling, with nothing else happening.
An incident is only named ('this was an incident') and the Sages could not release her without a get. A named-only incident of the kind Jeff called borderline.
Two reports of how many wedding blessings Levi and Rav Asi recited, cited as evidence of practice. Bare reports that lead nowhere.
A case comes before Rav Yosef, he rules, Abaye challenges and he clarifies. Coming before a rabbi plus a ruling and ordinary scholarly debate.
A betrothed couple comes before Rav Yosef and state claims. Coming before a rabbi is the only event; the rest is claims and ruling.
Rav Avya visits Neharde'a, sees a bolt tied with a reed, and rules. A setting that only frames a ruling is not enough.

Rabbi Hanina's habitual gift, then one day his wife delivers it, overhears the pauper's luxury, and he responds. A habit followed by a one-time event and a change; segments 4 onward are legal discussion and Mishnah.
Transmission of a ruling and Rav Mordekhai's recollection of a question put to Rav Ashi on a step. A question and answer about attribution, with no event beyond speech and no real conflict.
A dialogue in which an Amorite mocks a resident of Eretz Yisrael about the palm's yield and is rebutted. Speech only, but with conflict.
Ravina visits Mehoza, his host shows him a knife, and he tells him to take it to Rava. A setting framing a halakhic exchange.
Rava falls silent and afterward reasons with himself about the answer he could have given. Ordinary scholarly reasoning, with no event beyond speech.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim, and Rav Nahman orders him flogged. Mainly speech, though an act (flogging) is ordered; Jeff called Ketubot 10a borderline as mainly speech acts.
Rav Ashi's practice with wedding blessings at Rav Kahana's house is reported as evidence for the halakha. A report of practice that leads nowhere.
An amoraic dispute, then 'there was an incident' of a man who betrothed and fled, and Rafram ruled. The incident is only alluded to; weak, but there is a real event.
A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, they dispute the timing, and Rav Nahman rules. A real seizure plus a dispute and ruling; thinner than the stole-and-sold case.
Me'oret made her slave perform three of the acts and he died, cited only as an objection. Events with causality and change, but alluded to in one line.
Mareimar's practice of blocking Sura's alleyways with nets, with his reason. A report of practice with nothing following.
Mainly a riddling exchange, but it implies a real event: Rabbi Abbahu fled south after consulting the Nasi. Speech dominates, so borderline at most.
Rava's habitual practice when cases came before him; a custom with no one-time event following.
Rav's visit to Apsetaya and his prohibition are cited only as evidence of a ruling; one act and a ruling, nothing follows.
A woman comes before Ameimar, the brothers speak and he stays silent; cited as evidence of his view, with no further action or change.
A sharecropper took onions from the field and betrothed a woman with them, then Rava ruled; close to the stole-and-sold shape, but essentially one incident and a ruling, followed by legal commentary.
A bare report of Rav Zevid's ruling or his own act, cited for the halakha; nothing follows.
A teaching and a sage laughing at it; scholarly reaction, no event.
A one-line wonder: a fox nested in a turnip, which was weighed. Two events with weak causality and little change, cited as evidence for an exegetical claim.
Ravina comes before Rav Ashi with a question and gets a ruling; one situation and a ruling, nothing narrated as changing afterwards.
A man's conditional statement and later claim, followed by legal analysis; speech and a legal case, no ruling act or change.
A question put to the Judeans and their answer about a reading; question and answer only.
A found bill of divorce, an investigation by the Sages and testimony are real events, but they lead only into the Abaye/Rava legal discussion with no narrated outcome.
Two sages parting exchange halakhic teachings; a setting plus teaching speech, without conflict or event.
Rav Hisda's daughter asks and he answers; a dialogue without conflict or event.
The Madonite wished to give gifts, was advised, acquired land, made the gift, died, and the Sages carried out his words: several actions and a change.
A historical note that returnees camped by the well and were permitted it by custom; a report cited for the law, nothing develops.
A drought, everyone sold their mansions, wheat arrived, and Rav Nahman ordered the mansions returned: several events, a change, and a ruling that changes ownership.
Mar Yehuda poses a contradiction, the others are silent, and Rabba resolves it; ordinary scholarly back-and-forth, speech only.
Rabbi Zeira avoiding his teacher because he wanted to go up to the Land of Israel implies conflict and change, but it is only alluded to as a lead-in to Rav Yehuda's dictum.
A man sold his mother's ketubah, she died, and he contested the sale; real events and conflict, but resolved only in Rami bar Hama and Rava's legal discussion.
A report of R. Abbahu's habitual practice in two places, cited as evidence and then discussed; nothing happens and nothing follows.
Rav's visit and examination is a single act alluded to as evidence in the legal argument, with no response or change.
An exegetical derivation of the dates of Moses' birth and death; no narrated incident.
An incident only named, in which Rabbi gave an orphan one-twelfth; a single ruling with no other action or change, used to reconcile sources.
A one-line eyewitness report (an Arab cut open his camel and it died at once) with two actions and a change, but cited as evidence inside legal discussion.
Parallel to the 65a courtroom scene: a widow comes before Rav Yosef, he apportions food and wine, and she retorts about silk; mainly dialogue with apportioning as the action.
A question and a cryptic answer; speech only, with no conflict and no narrated event.

Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to act, an old woman reports Rav Nahman's prohibition, and Rav Pappi rebukes them; mainly dialogue and legal discussion with some events and an implied change, plus a one-line alluded incident.
A case came before R. Yitzhak in Antioch and he ruled; coming before a rabbi is the only event.
Two rabbis stand up when R. Shimon bar Abba passes and he objects; real actions but mainly speech with little change.
A man comes to R. Hanina with a question and receives an answer; a setting plus question and answer is not a story.
A woman obligated to an oath in Rav Beivai's court, the litigant's demand, her request and the order to write the document, then Rav Pappi's sharp retort; after she comes to court it is all dialogue.
R. Yirmeya travels to the villages, cannot answer their question, and on returning learns the answer in the study hall; real movement and a small change, but mainly a question and answer.
Judges in Nehardea and Pumbedita ruled and collected, and Rav Nahman threatened to seize their houses unless they reversed; rulings that act on property plus conflict, but no narrated outcome.
Judges ruled, Reish Lakish reversed their action, and R. Yohanan criticized him; acts that change something plus conflict, but brief and immediately used for legal discussion.
A woman before R. Ami is refused, argues, and he reverses and rules to compel divorce; a court scene with conflict and change carried mainly by dialogue.
A son-in-law passed his in-laws' door and Rav Sheshet flogged him; two actions linked causally, but minimal and cited as evidence.
Rabbi went to study with R. Elazar ben Shamua, the students ganged up on him and prevented him, and he learned only one thing; actions, conflict and a consequence.
The Sages apportioned 400 gold coins for perfume to Nakdimon's daughter; she responded with a barbed blessing and they answered amen. An apportioning act followed mainly by speech.
First-person reports of being given food at Shmuel's and Rav Kahana's tables when they would otherwise have been endangered; minimal events cited as evidence for the rule.
A found bill of divorce is sent as a question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and answered with a ruling; nothing changes beyond the question and ruling, cited as proof in a legal argument.

A briefly told incident: Mar Zutra compelled a rebellious wife and Rabbi Hanina of Sura was born of the union; there is an act and an outcome, but it is sketched as a precedent with little development.
A ruling requiring doors on an alleyway in Neharde'a, followed by legal analysis; no narrated event beyond the ruling.
Rabbi Hanina's habitual gift is followed by a one-time event: his wife delivers it, observes the pauper's luxury and reports back, leading to his response.
Ulla dies abroad, the news reaches Rabbi Elazar, who laments, is told the coffin is coming, and responds; events with a reaction and development.
A testimony about a household practice (buying brine with tithe money) and a scholarly reply, cited in legal argument; a bare report of practice.
A testator's will and the estate he left set up a legal case that is then only discussed; no further narrated action or change.
Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Elazar and afterwards commented on it; a ruling and a statement, cited as legal evidence, with no narrated event.
Mar Yehuda instructs townspeople about their eiruv and Rava rebukes him; instruction and ordinary scholarly rebuke, no change follows.
Rava's boast and a sage's halakhic question with Rava's reply; speech only, ordinary scholarly exchange within the passage.
Several events (purchase, collateral given, price rises, sellers seek to cancel) then a ruling by Rabbi Ami; more than one event and a change, but it ends in a ruling with nothing after.
Only an allusion that teachings were said in two places on one Shabbat, used as a legal proof; the alluded content is speech, not a narrated event.
A halakhic question, a search for a source and a ruling sent out; scholarly process and legal discussion rather than a narrated incident.
A man sets a divorce condition, returns but is blocked by the ferry and calls out, then Shmuel rules; real events with some drama, ending in a ruling.
Rava poses a question and Rav Nahman is silent; speech in ordinary scholarly exchange, followed by Gemara commentary.
Rav Dimi's silence, Abaye's answer and Rav Dimi's praise; standard dialogue with no event or conflict.
R. Hiyya bar Abba encounters R. Yehoshua ben Levi rushing his grandson to synagogue, asks why, and thereafter changes his own conduct; events, response and lasting change.
An incident in Rav Hisda's study hall is only mentioned, not narrated, and the passage is the legal resolution from a mishna.
The blind man is late, a messenger is sent, they cross paths, the messenger reports adultery, and the man comes before Shmuel; a sequence of events with consequences and a ruling.
Rabbi Akiva's etrog tithing is a bare report of what he did, cited as evidence; ruled not a story by the editor.
A report of Rav Hisda's practice of refusing to rule, cited as evidence; nothing follows from it.
Elijah's advice to Rabbi Natan is pure speech, with no event and no conflict.
A divorce document is sent to Rabba as a question and he rules; nothing else is narrated.
A yevama comes before Rabbi Tarfon and he instructs the students, cited as a precedent; the instruction is speech and nothing changes.
Rav Safra's and Rava's habitual Shabbat preparations are a custom cited as evidence and lead nowhere.
The Sages propose permitting the Gibeonites and Rabbi answers rhetorically; it is a halakhic exchange with no event beyond speech.
Rav Yosef acts on Rav's view and Shmuel takes offense with a sarcastic retort: one real act and an emotional reaction, but mainly speech. Segment 3 is the Gemara's analysis.
Rav reports having seen Rabbi Hiyya use a laced sandal, cited as evidence for practice; nothing follows.
Rabbi Elazar puts a halakhic question to an elder; this is speech only, with no event narrated.
Levi teaches in two attributions and is first not praised, then praised, which is a change in his reception, but it is all teaching and speech.
A debtor sells two fields, the creditor seizes one and comes for the other, and the purchaser brings money and confronts him: several actions with conflict and a change.
People cast aspersions on two men and a rabbi rules on each; there is no further action or change.
The Sages switch the attributions and send the question to Rav, who swears an oath in response. The events are quasi-speech, but there is implied conflict over Shmuel.
Jeff named Mar Zutra's practice of writing the halitza passage as a bare report with no continuation.
A father sends his son for chicks and the son fulfills both mitzvot, then falls and dies: an incident with actions and a change. The exegetical conclusion is the Gemara's commentary.
The Gemara quotes the Mishnah incident: the Sages' boat sails on Shabbat and they respond in different ways. A Talmudic citation of a Mishnah story can be included.
Rav Aha meets Rav Ashi's students and asks a question, and they answer; a setting plus a question and answer is not a story.
One real event, the death of Nehunya's son, is told as a coda to the preceding story and then becomes exegesis; it is part of a story, with little narrated here.
A heretic taunts Rabban Gamliel and he retorts: speech with real conflict, but no event beyond speaking.
Rav Hisda praises Rav Hamnuna, he comes to Rav Huna, who sees his uncovered head, turns his face away and bans him until he marries: several actions, conflict and a change.
Mainly a sent question and a reply, but one real event intervenes (Rav Huna dies before it arrives) and his son answers instead; mostly speech.
The maidservant's immersion is cited inside a legal challenge: one incident and Rabbi's ruling, with no further narrated change; Jeff's 2026-10-25 limit makes that not a story.
Rav Yehuda's practice and Ulla's advice citing others' practice; a habit plus counsel with no event or change following.
A ruling and a scholarly challenge citing a written list; legal discussion, no event.
Rav Huna found the Sages sitting and debating and he answered them; ordinary scholarly dialogue, the setting only frames the argument.
Habitual practices of Michal and Jonah's wife cited as legal evidence; customs that lead nowhere (and biblical figures).
A bare report that Bonyam sent Rabbi fine linens, then lexical explanation; one act, no continuation.
Pure speech, but a personal reproach of Ben Azzai for not marrying and his defense carries conflict beyond routine debate.
A man comes before Rabban Gamliel with a claim and receives a parable-ruling; coming before the rabbi is the only event.
Only names the location of the Mishnah's incident as a legal answer; nothing is narrated.
Rava rules Mari bar Rachel fit and also appoints him an official, an act beyond the ruling, followed by legal justification.
Rabbi Yohanan's reminiscences of studying with Rabbi Oshaya and seating density, with Gemara discussion; reports with no event or change.
Two incidents: a man removes a feather from Ameimar / covers spittle before Mar Ukva, is questioned, and the judge disqualifies himself; action, response and change.
A baraita recited and Rabbi Yohanan rejecting it; ordinary scholarly exchange.
Ravina sees a man desecrating Shabbat, protests, is ignored, excommunicates him, then asks Rav Ashi about it; multiple actions and change.
Rabbi Abbahu teaches and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi turn their faces in disagreement; mainly speech with a gesture of conflict, cited as evidence and analyzed.
An encounter with Elijah that only frames a question and answer of exegesis; setting plus Q&A is not a story.
Rabbi's deathbed pronouncements embed a full incident: the people of Bireta DeSatya fished on Shabbat, were excommunicated, and became apostates.
A habitual practice (following Rabbi Yohanan to eat Genosar fruit, his customary oath) cited for a legal point; no one-time event follows.
Part of the narrative of Rabbi's death: he summons his sons, they enter, he transmits wisdom and the office of Nasi; actions and change.
The impotence notices are bare reports, but Rav Aha bar Yaakov's illness, suspension from the cedar and healing are real events with change, though minimal and cited as illustration.
A fragment of exegetical argument about Joshua 5:11; no narrated incident, and the referent is biblical.
A man comes before R. Yehoshua ben Levi, question and answer, and a status ruling; a case before a rabbi and his ruling is not a story.
One event (Nehemya straying beyond the limit) followed by a ruling on what to do; no outcome is narrated.
R. Zeira's arrival only frames a reported teaching; setting plus teaching is speech, not a story.
Rava pours drinks at his son's wedding, some sages stand and others do not, and he becomes angry: several actions, conflict and an emotional reaction.
A man comes before R. Yosei with a question and receives a ruling with its scriptural basis; nothing else happens.
A bare report that Rabba ruled in practice on a found bill of divorce, followed by disagreement on the details.
Rabbi falls ill, R. Hiyya visits and finds him weeping (events and emotion), but the passage is mainly a question and answer with a quoted baraita.
Pishon's wife's refusal is mentioned as a single event in a debate, without change or causality (ruled not by the editor).
A deposit, the heirs' claim and the woman's counterclaim are events, but after she comes before Rav Nahman it is dialogue and a ruling with no change narrated.
A woman comes to court and is advised how to appear; nothing further is narrated, then legal discussion.
An incident cited as precedent: a case came before Rav Yehuda and he ruled; no further action or change.
Shmuel's instruction to Rav Hana is speech cited as evidence of his view.
A habitual charitable practice reported and then analysed; the custom leads nowhere.
Rav walks among sheaves and remarks on them; one act plus a saying, no change, followed by dicta.
Bare reports that items were brought to Levi, Zeiri and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, with no continuation.
A complimentary remark in scholarly dialogue; speech only.
A student's liability and the Rabbis' statement to spare him; no narrated event beyond the ruling.
A man comes before R. Meir about an onion eiruv and R. Meir confines him to his four cubits, a ruling that is itself an act changing the man's situation.
Only the opening of a sent question; a question and answer with no event and no conflict.
Rabbi Tarfon's habitual service of his mother leads to a one-time event: he boasts in the study hall and is rebuked, with a vivid counter-example.
A real incident (a bequest, the orphans divide the estate and withhold the palm) followed by legal discussion and a proposed remedy; events with little narrated change.
A prolonged dispute between the schools resolved by a vote; mainly speech, but with conflict and a decision that changes things.
An incident (the Yavne reservoir measured and found deficient) leads to a dispute between Tarfon and Akiva that ends with Tarfon conceding and praising Akiva; event, conflict and change.
Ravin goes to betroth a woman for his son and betroths her himself; several actions and a change, with the Gemara's justification attached.
Ravina examines a knife in his teacher's region and Rav Ashi challenges him; one real act followed mainly by dialogue with some conflict. Segments 2-3 are bare reports.
Exegesis on a biblical verse explaining how virgins were identified; no narrated event of the catalogue's kind.
Ketubot 50b: the orphan daughters come before Shmuel and he orders sustenance; coming before a rabbi and a ruling, nothing else changes.
Statements and habitual practices about orla cited as evidence; no event that leads anywhere.
A case comes before Rabbi Yohanan, an exchange follows, and Reish Lakish looks harshly at Rabbi Elazar and rebukes him; mainly speech, but with conflict and an emotional reaction.
An alluded practice of drawing water from the Tzippori channel, cited as legal evidence; a custom with no event following.
Bar Shatya's sale and conflicting witnesses, cited as a legal precedent and resolved by a ruling; a case and a ruling with no further narrated change.
A man snatches coins from another and throws them to a woman as betrothal, then comes before Rava who rules; several actions followed by a ruling, like the cow case.
A setting (Abbahu leaning on his attendant) framing a series of halakhic questions and answers; a setting plus Q&A is not a story.
An incident only alluded to (a husband abroad, a twelve-month pregnancy) and Rava Tosfa'a's ruling declaring the child fit, cited for legal analysis.
Ameimar permits a marriage and Rav Ashi challenges his source; a ruling and ordinary scholarly back-and-forth.
Rabbi Tavla saw a bolt and said nothing, cited as legal evidence; a bare report with nothing following.
Rav Pappa forces Yehuda bar Mareimar into the house, his silence makes Abba of Sura write over all his property, and the exchange that follows; multiple actions, misunderstanding and change.
An incident alluded to, in which Rafram presses Rav Ashi and Rav Ashi exacts full payment; a ruling that is itself an act, but the incident is barely told.
Rabbi acts on a ruling, is challenged by Perata and reverses it: an action and a change, but the substance is a ruling and its retraction, so borderline.
A couple comes before Rava, he rules, is challenged with a baraita and retracts; coming before him is the only event, the rest is ruling and speech.
Mention that Abaye and Rava disagreed about a balcony all their lives is cited as evidence; no incident is narrated.
Rabban Gamliel's levirate marriage with his daughter's rival wife is cited as a legal precedent with no response or development; a bare report used as evidence.
Rabbi Elazar goes to Shmuel's lodging to verify a teaching and confronts him, Shmuel falls silent: mainly speech with some action and a challenge.
Rav Pappa instructed Pappa the ox herder to trace his name: a single ruling/practice reported as precedent, nothing follows.
Within Rabbi's deathbed statements is an embedded incident: the people of Bireta DeSatya fished on Shabbat, Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them, and they apostatized, with actions and change.
Rabbi Hiyya and Bar Kappara jump up and swear opposing oaths about what they heard from Rabbi: dramatic conflict, but mainly speech and argument; segments 8-15 are Gemara analysis (R-B4).
An incident of ten men carrying a woman out on a bier is only alluded to as evidence for Rav's ruling; per R-C6 an alluded incident is borderline.
A question and answer between Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav about abstaining from labor; speech without conflict or event.
Rav Nahman found two scholars debating in the marketplace and disagreed with them: a setting framing standard scholarly dialogue.
Abaye reminds Rav Yosef of a teaching he had forgotten; ordinary scholarly exchange with no narrated event.
Rav Safra's objections, Abaye's silence and Rav Yosef's suggested answer are ordinary Talmudic back-and-forth, not conflict in R-C2's sense.
A man betrothed with rags and Rav Shimi assessed its value: a case brought for a ruling with no further narrated action or change.
Rabbi Eliezer missed the study hall and asked Rabbi Asi what was said; a setting plus question and answer.
Rava's coercing Rav Natan bar Ami to give 400 zuz is a one-line report cited as precedent, with no development.
The ketubah was lost, the couple came before Rav Yosef, and the rest is a ruling and its revision; the order to write a new one only implies an outcome.
Rav Pappa serves drinks at his son's wedding, Rav Yitzhak fails to stand, and Rav Pappa becomes angry: actions, conflict and an emotional reaction, though brief and cited as evidence.
Rabbi Elazar ascends to Israel, is ordained and seated in the intercalation council, responding each time; real events but little causality or drama.
Rav Beivai corrects Rav Yosef's attribution and Rav Yosef realizes his error: scholarly dialogue about transmission, no narrated event.
The sons' freeing is the only event; the rest is a ruling and a scholarly challenge, with nothing changing afterwards.
A document brought before a rabbi, his inclination to validate and a colleague's correction: a case and a ruling, no further narrated action.
A question and answer to R. Yehoshua plus testimony about families' lineage cited as halakhic evidence; no event follows.
A visit and the act of placing the granddaughter on his lap, then a pointed exchange of halakhic rebukes; mainly speech but a real event occurs.
All dialogue about the correct text of a baraita, then Shmuel's admonition; teaching and correcting are speech, no event.
Gemara's resolution of a contradiction by dating Rav's statements; no narrative.
Habitual practices of R. Yohanan and Rava cited as halakhic evidence; nothing follows.
Rava's collection on two notes cited as a precedent, followed by legal analysis; a bare report.
An insult from a heretic and the sage's retort: speech only, but with real conflict beyond ordinary scholarly debate.
A betrothal with silk serves only as the case for an amoraic dispute; one event, then legal discussion.
R. Ami declares a neighbour a mamzer, the man goes about weeping, and R. Ami responds to console him: several actions, emotion and change.
The daughters-in-law rebel, Rabbi sends Sages to examine them, and the women's retort shows their refusal: several events and a response.
Shmuel throwing lentil bread to his dog is a one-line report cited as evidence about the bread's edibility; it leads nowhere.
The widow and the guard incident is only alluded to and must be filled in from the commentaries, which is borderline.
A habitual manner of speech of R. Abbahu, no event.
Rav Kahana prompts Rav Ashi, who first does not remember, later remembers and testifies, notices Rav Kahana's hesitation and reassures him: actions and change.
A couple comes before Rav Nahman, who identifies her by accent and rules, then reverses on being challenged; a case and ruling with a little more dynamism than a bare ruling.
Rav Pappa goes to write the marriage contract, Yehuda bar Mareimar comes out to greet him and takes leave at the door; real events but little change within the passage.
A testator's instruction and a price change are the legal case for a ruling; nothing else is narrated.
An incident brought before Rav Yehuda and his ruling, cited as evidence in a legal discussion; no further action or change.
Rav Ami's permission, the Sages' objection and his answer are speech with some conflict and implied change; no event beyond speaking.
Rav Hisda's statement about his own early marriage is a dictum, not a narrated incident.
An incident (the master was forced to free a half-slave woman) is cited briefly as evidence and then discussed legally; events are present but barely narrated.
Mar Shmuel's permission to use a mortar is a ruling about a household object; nothing happens or changes.
Costly burials led people to abandon their dead until Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in linen and everyone followed: actions, causality and change.
Rav corrects a teacher's version of the mishna and the Gemara explains it; ordinary scholarly exchange and teaching.
R. Elazar's habit of leaving his cloak while absorbed in Torah leads to a one-time event: a man came to take it and found a serpent guarding it.
The widow sues the orphans, they object to her dress, she puts on all her clothes, and Ravina rules they are appraised: several actions with a consequence.
One event (the slave immersed a gentile woman) followed only by Rav Yosef's ruling; nothing else happens.
Embedded in the brothers' letter is an incident of a man who wished to leave the Land for a woman, heard this teaching, and stayed suffering until his death.
A man states where he is from and R. Yitzhak identifies the place, followed by legal discussion; speech without conflict or change.
A woman's mispronounced sentence cited as a linguistic example; a single speech act with no event or change.
R. Yannai sharply rebukes R. Hanina Kara's ruling; a rebuke is ordinary Talmudic discourse, with no event beyond speech.
Rava appoints an amora and publicly retracts his earlier teaching; a real act and a change, but mainly a teaching speech.
An exegetical account of how the Midianite girls were tested before the High Priest's frontplate, built on a biblical episode.
A hypothetical scenario the Gemara constructs to resolve a legal difficulty; not an event.
A man had witnesses trace their names on ordinary documents and Rav Kahana had him flogged; an act and a consequence, but told in one line.
A deathbed bequest, then Toviya comes and R. Yohanan rules; a case before a rabbi and his ruling with nothing further changing.
A woman comes before Rava and a cross-examination follows that changes his ruling; mostly dialogue, but it leads to a change.
Ravina's collection for Rav Ashi's daughter is cited as a legal precedent, a report of what was done with nothing following.
